cards.front: {{c1::Symbiosis}} is a close relationship between individuals of different species living together, often for a long time.
cards.quote: Symbiosis is a close relationship between individuals of different species living together, often for a long time.

cards.front: A hawk catches a mouse in one quick attack. Why is that not symbiosis?
cards.back: Symbiosis needs a close relationship of different species living together. A predator catching prey is a brief meeting, not living together.
cards.quote: Scope: use this rule for close relationships between individuals of different species living together, not for brief meetings such as a predator catching prey.

cards.front: {{c1::Mutualism}} is symbiosis in which all the partners benefit.
cards.quote: Mutualism is symbiosis in which all the partners benefit.

cards.front: {{c1::Commensalism}} is symbiosis in which one partner benefits and the others are unaffected.
cards.quote: Commensalism is symbiosis in which one partner benefits and the others are unaffected.

cards.front: {{c1::Parasitism}} is symbiosis in which one partner benefits and the others are harmed.
cards.quote: Parasitism is symbiosis in which one partner benefits and the others are harmed.

cards.front: What is a lichen made of?
cards.back: A fungus and an alga or a cyanobacterium living as one body. A cyanobacterium is a bacterium that can make its own food.
cards.quote: A lichen is a fungus and an alga or a cyanobacterium (a bacterium that can make its own food) living as one body.

cards.front: What two steps should you take before choosing a kind of symbiosis for a pair of species?
cards.back: Name both partners and record each partner's outcome (helped, unaffected or harmed). Then pick the category.
cards.quote: Key idea: name both partners and record each outcome before choosing a category.

cards.front: In a model of two species living together, both are set to harmed. Does this match mutualism, commensalism or parasitism?
cards.back: No. In all three kinds, at least one partner is helped.
cards.why: Each definition has at least one partner that benefits.
cards.quote: No. In all three kinds, at least one partner is helped.

cards.front: In a Virginia lichen, what does the fungus get and what does the alga get?
cards.back: The fungus gets food. The alga gets shelter and water. This is mutualism.
cards.quote: Inside it, both main partners gain.

cards.front: Bacteria in soybean root bumps get food from the plant. They turn nitrogen from the air into a form the plant can use. Which kind of symbiosis is this?
cards.quote: It is mutualism because both partners gain.

cards.front: Why is a lichen on tree bark called commensalism, and why is that kind hard to prove?
cards.back: The lichen gets a place to live and the tree seems unaffected. "Seems unaffected" means no one has measured any harm or help, so it is hard to prove.
cards.quote: "Seems unaffected" means no one has measured any harm or help.

cards.front: In parasitism, what is the host?
cards.back: The living thing that the other partner lives on or in. The parasite benefits by feeding on it.
cards.quote: In parasitism, the host is the living thing that the other partner lives on or in.

cards.front: A blacklegged tick feeds on a deer's blood for several days. The deer stays alive and loses blood. Is the tick a parasite or a predator?
cards.back: A parasite. A parasite usually does not kill its host and feeds for days or longer. A predator usually kills its prey in a brief attack.
cards.quote: The main difference: a parasite usually does not kill its host.

cards.front: A classmate says fungi help tree roots because they are being kind. How does science explain why such partnerships last?
cards.back: Partners that lived together survived and reproduced better than ones that lived apart. So over many generations the partnership carried on. Kindness is not required.
cards.quote: In mutualism, partners that lived together survived and reproduced better than ones that lived apart.

cards.front: Why can a parasite partnership carry on even though the host is harmed?
cards.back: Partners that lived this way survived and reproduced better, so over many generations the relationship carried on, although the host is harmed.
cards.quote: A parasite can carry on the same way, although its host is harmed.

cards.front: A lichen grows on bare rock. Why might the alga alone or the fungus alone do poorly there?
cards.back: The alga alone might dry out. The fungus alone would have no food, because no fungus can make its own.
cards.quote: There, the alga alone might dry out, and the fungus alone would have no food, because no fungus can make its own.

cards.front: A root fungus brings minerals from soil into a plant's roots, and the plant passes it food. Why is that only a prediction about benefit to the plant?
cards.back: It stays a prediction until evidence shows the plant really benefits, such as a growth test with and without the fungus.
cards.quote: That trade is only a prediction until evidence shows the plant really benefits.

cards.front: In the marigold greenhouse test at 25% water, mean shoot dry mass was 2.62 g with root fungus and 2.01 g without. How much more mass, and about what percent more, with the fungus?
cards.back: Difference: 2.62 - 2.01 = 0.61 g. Percent more: 0.61 / 2.01 x 100 is about 30%.
cards.why: The mass without fungus is the comparison, so it goes in the denominator.
cards.quote: The mass without fungus is the comparison, so it belongs in the denominator.
cards.section: Evidence: does a root fungus help a plant grow?

cards.front: In the marigold test at 100% water, mean shoot dry mass was 5.29 g with fungus and 4.44 g without. Find the difference and the percent more with fungus.
cards.back: Difference: 5.29 - 4.44 = 0.85 g. Percent more: 0.85 / 4.44 x 100 is about 19%. The gap in grams is largest here, but the percent gap is smaller than at 25% water (about 30%).
cards.quote: The gap in grams is largest at 100% water.
cards.section: Evidence: does a root fungus help a plant grow?

cards.front: In a fungus test, every fungus pot sits by a bright window and every control pot sits farther away. Can a mass difference be credited to the fungus?
cards.back: No. Light and fungus both changed, so either could explain the result. Mix the groups together on the shelf.
cards.quote: Light and fungus both changed, so either could explain the result.

cards.front: Plan a fair test of whether a root fungus helps bean plants grow. What is the control, what stays constant, and how many plants per group?
cards.back: Control: pots with the same potting mix and the same amount of heat-killed powder, so the only difference is living fungus. Constants: seeds, pot size, potting mix, water, light and temperature. At least 10 pots per group, mixed on the shelf so neither group gets better light.
cards.quote: Trials: at least 10 pots per group, mixed on the shelf so neither group gets better light.

cards.front: In a test of trees with and without lichen, both groups of 10 trees grew a mean of 2.0 cm in a year, and the lichens grew. Which kind of symbiosis do these made-up data fit best?
cards.back: Commensalism: the lichen gains and the tree does not change. Equal means only show that no harm or help was measured, which is why commensalism is hard to prove.
cards.quote: In each case, check both outcomes before naming the relationship.

cards.front: In a 2022 study, 99 related wheat lines grew with the same mix of five root fungi. What does the range of shoot growth show about measuring symbiosis?
cards.back: Shoot growth ranged from 34% less to 89% more, and only 12 lines differed clearly from no change. The same partnership can turn out differently for different partners, so the effect must be measured, not assumed.
cards.quote: The effect must be measured, not assumed.
cards.section: Going deeper: when the simple model needs refining
